title: Teaching
text:
My teaching starts from a simple conviction: students learn research by doing real research. In my courses they design genuine experiments, analyze their own data, and write up the results. Across fifteen years and two countries, I have taught developmental psychology, research methods, and econometrics in face-to-face, hybrid, and online formats. My full teaching philosophy is here:.

title: Tamara Podvysotska
text:
Hello and welcome :)
I am a developmental scientist with a background in economics. I study how family economic circumstances shape children’s development and young adults’ life chances.
My research sits at the intersection of developmental science, economics, and policy. I completed my Ph.D. in Developmental Psychology at the University of Pittsburgh, where my dissertation followed more than 7,000 young adults over 24 years to examine how the composition and timing of childhood family wealth relate to outcomes across education, economic wellbeing, mental health, and family formation.
I bring an unusual path to this work: before turning to developmental science, I earned a doctorate in economics and spent a decade as a professor and policy researcher in Ukraine, advising national health and social reform efforts in partnership with the World Bank, WHO, and the World Economic Forum.
As an educator with fifteen years of university teaching across two countries, I teach developmental psychology, research methods, and quantitative analysis — helping students connect developmental science to the real economic and social conditions of children’s lives.
Learn more about me →

title: About
text:
My career has followed one question across two disciplines: how do economic conditions shape human wellbeing and development?
I began as an economist. After earning my Candidate of Sciences (Ph.D.) in Economics at the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine with a dissertation on health and economic growth, I spent nearly a decade as an Associate Professor of Finance & Econometrics at the National University “Kyiv-Mohyla Academy” while working as a policy researcher and analyst. In those years I co-authored Ukraine’s National Competitiveness Reports in partnership with the World Economic Forum, contributed to the healthcare and education chapters of Ukraine’s National Program of Economic Reforms, and coordinated analytical work with the World Bank, WHO, and international research institutes.
That policy work kept returning me to a developmental insight: economic circumstances matter most in childhood, when they shape the trajectories that adult policy later struggles to correct. To study those processes directly, I came to the University of Pittsburgh, where I completed my Ph.D. in Developmental Psychology (with a minor in Quantitative Methodology) in 2026, working with Dr. Elizabeth Votruba-Drzal. My dissertation examined the long-term associations of childhood family wealth — disaggregated into assets and debts — with young adults’ outcomes.

title: Curriculum Vitae
Research
text:
Wealth inequality is among the defining trends of the U.S. economy, yet most research on how family wealth shapes children’s development relies on net worth, a single composite number that conceals the distinct, sometimes opposing, roles of what families own and what they owe. My research unpacks that composite.
My dissertation drew on longitudinal data following more than 7,000 young adults over 24 years (NLSY79 and its Child and Young Adult cohort) to examine how parental assets and debts across three periods of childhood relate to fifteen young adult outcomes spanning education, economic wellbeing, mental health, behavior, and family formation. Three findings anchor this work. First, assets and debts are qualitatively distinct predictors, and treating them as a single net figure obscures how each operates. Second, timing matters: early-childhood wealth was linked to behavioral outcomes, middle childhood to mental health, and adolescence to educational, economic, and family formation outcomes. Third, young adults’ own wealth accumulation is a central pathway through which childhood economic conditions carry forward — and assets and debts persist across generations more strongly than net worth itself.
This work extends an earlier research program in health economics: before studying wealth and child development, I spent a decade examining how health, poverty, and inequality interact in transition economies, in research supported by the Vienna Institute of International Economic Studies and the Global Development Network and in policy work with the World Bank, WHO, and the World Economic Forum.
